name: Umar Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and this conversation is confidential. What is an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the carpentry on cottage renovations, often lifting boards into lofts and building dormer frames beside old rafters. My trade certificate got me started, and years of awkward roofs taught me where to measure twice. Seeing a dark loft turn into a room still pleases me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is difficult outside the building work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Denise, my wife, does garage office work part-time, and our children are grown. My pay is low, we have less than a month saved and the van repairs are on a card. There are few nearby builders, my shoulder aches, and I have never used AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the cottage loft still needs a carpenter who can see what the old rafters will carry. The office can save time on quotes, but I have no reason to change my tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Denise works part-time at a garage office, and our grown children are on their own. We have under a month saved and my lead pay is low; a quiet AI future does nothing about the van repair bill or the ache in my shoulder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep cutting loft joists and checking the old roof with a level. I would ask Gary, my boss, for two paid Saturday jobs this winter and use those wages to pay extra on the van repair debt if the work comes through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the money is already thin. The van repair bill wakes me up more than any AI forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How urgent is the van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It starts, but tyres and brake repair went on a card. If it stops, I cannot reach village jobs, so I need to clear that bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI tool for a quote?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used one. Gary can handle the office quote while I measure the loft.

say: I would tell the crew **old cottage roofs** still need a carpenter’s judgement.
I would leave small **office quote savings** to Gary.
think: Our **van debt** and less than one month saved keep finances tense.
My **shoulder pain** makes coming working years uncertain even without AI change.
do: Keep **cottage loft work** and check rafters with a level.
Pay extra **van debt** from two paid Saturday jobs only if Gary offers them.
S0.quote: The van repair bill wakes me up more than any AI forecast.
fieldNote: His baseline anxiety comes from **van debt** and low pay, with few local jobs.
Extra debt reduction depends on **paid Saturday work**, not simply moving current savings.

steps.text: Keep fitting cottage loft joists and measuring old rafters
Pay extra van debt only from two paid Saturday jobs if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can order plasterboard quicker, but it cannot carry sheets up that narrow cottage stair. I would want Gary to check the new schedule before sending us two sites in one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office work may change first, then Gary might use faster quotes to promise more jobs than our small crew can finish. My hours could become stop-start, and Denise’s garage pay will not carry both of us if my weeks shorten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the next two rosters with paid hours and ask Gary which jobs are confirmed. If the hours fall, Denise and I would postpone the planned bedroom carpet before we touch the small reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I know how to fit a dormer, but I cannot make an empty Friday on a cottage site into a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Gary about the schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Give me the signed customer date and enough paid time to finish the loft safely. I would not rush a roof opening because a computer found a spare afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you seek another local job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not before hours actually fall. There are few builders nearby, and I would need a posted job with a firm wage before leaving Gary.

say: I would ask Gary for **confirmed customer dates** before AI makes a two-site schedule.
I would keep **roof openings safe** despite faster quotes.
think: My **paid weeks** could become uneven if Gary overbooks a small crew.
Denise’s **part-time garage wage** cannot replace my earnings for long.
do: Compare two **rosters and paid hours** with confirmed jobs.
Delay the **bedroom carpet** if hours fall before using savings.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible cut to my weekly pay.
S1.quote: I cannot make an empty Friday on a cottage site into a wage.
fieldNote: His concern is a **small-firm schedule gap**, not immediate robot carpentry.
The carpet delay follows **measured lost hours**, protecting a very thin household reserve before winter.

steps.text: Delay bedroom carpet only if two rosters show fewer paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Gary that thinking AI in 2028 can draw a loft, but a robot will not fit it until around 2031. I would never let a machine try the first cut above a family’s bedroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some small renovation firms to lose jobs when capable robots arrive, and Gary could be one of them. If his orders fall, I could lose most of my low wage with less than a month saved and almost no nearby work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid loft shifts while they exist and ask Gary for confirmed jobs in writing. If two rosters show serious cuts, I would apply to posted carpentry work farther away only if firm pay covers travel and bills; I would not quit a paid loft job for a rumour about another site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would lie awake counting how many weeks the van and food bills can survive without my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train to operate a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a contractor posts a paid operator job, funds the course and pays training hours. I would need to see the machine isolated and tested before getting near a moving arm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not before Denise and I look at the accounts and real job offers. The children have their own bills, and I would not make a promise they have not offered.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** draws lofts before 2031 robots can make hands-on cuts.
I would reject a first **robot trial** above an occupied bedroom.
think: I expect some **small firms** to lose work and Gary’s crew could be cut.
The **tiny reserve** and few nearby jobs make a large wage loss frightening.
do: Keep **paid loft shifts** while Gary has confirmed work.
Apply to **posted distant carpentry jobs** after two cut rosters only for firm travel-and-bills-covering pay.
**Train** for a posted paid operator job only with funded paid study and an isolated, tested machine.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major income loss and a near-empty reserve.
S2.quote: I would not quit a paid loft job for a rumour about another site.
fieldNote: He expects a possible **firm-level loss** after the robot lag and describes sleepless money worry.
A distant search requires **posted work** and firm net pay, while course enquiry alone is not retraining.

steps.text: Keep paid cottage loft shifts while Gary has confirmed work
Apply to posted distant carpentry jobs after two cut rosters for firm travel-and-bills-covering pay
Train on isolated tested robot only for posted paid operator job with funded paid training hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Gary five years gives us time to test a fitting robot on a crooked cottage loft before it enters a customer’s bedroom. I would still want the saw isolated while the crew marks a safe area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 changes drawings and quotes first, while capable robots arrive around 2034. I will be sixty six then and may still need work because the van debt and thin reserve have delayed any clear retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading paid renovation shifts next year. If a nearby builder posts a paid quality-check role with a wage covering our bills and offers funded training on paid time, I would take the course and apply; otherwise I would keep fitting lofts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though five years gives me time to see whether a real job appears. I will not buy a robot-check course for a vacancy that exists only in a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A week without wages would empty too much of our reserve. Any trial would need paid hours and the machine powered down before a person checks a fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire if the new role is unavailable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Denise and I can cover household costs from real income and savings. A robot date does not make the accounts work.

say: I would ask for a **crooked-loft trial** before 2034 fitting robots enter occupied cottages.
I would start with the **saw isolated** before anyone checks a fault.
think: At sixty six I may still need **paid carpentry work**.
Our **van debt** and tiny reserve make retirement timing uncertain.
do: Keep **paid renovation shifts** next year while offered.
Complete **funded quality-check training** only for posted nearby bill-covering job with paid time.
feel: **Anxious** about future work, with a conditional paid option.
S3.quote: I will not buy a robot-check course for a vacancy that exists only in a brochure.
fieldNote: He would take actual training only for a **funded paid role**.
The safety condition keeps dangerous equipment **powered down** before anyone approaches a failed cut.

steps.text: Keep paid cottage renovation shifts next year
Complete funded checker course only for posted nearby bill-covering job with paid time
Apply for posted nearby checker role only if bill-covering pay follows funded training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger carpenters a decade is enough to learn how an old cottage roof is put together before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. I would teach them to check the timber before cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty eight at the thinking date and seventy one at the robot date. Denise and I hope I can stop heavy loft work before then, but with little saved today that depends on paid years and how my shoulder holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep loft jobs during 2026 and send an extra small amount from each paid week to the van debt only after rent and food are covered. In the first year after 2036, if we can afford retirement I would not book site shifts; if not, I would take only paid ground-level tasks my shoulder allows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today’s money, though the long timetable gives a little breathing room. I cannot use a ten-year warning to pay next month’s garage bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra would go to the van debt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten from each paid week when Denise’s garage hours and household bills allow. If either wage falls, I would keep that money for food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this card make you retire early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have no firm funded date. Denise and I will decide from actual household income and my health.

say: I would teach **old-roof carpentry** before 2036 thinking AI and 2039 robots change sites.
I would keep **timber checks** in apprentice training.
think: Retirement before **2036** depends on paid years and my shoulder.
Our **thin savings** make current bills anxious despite a long warning.
do: Keep **2026 paid loft work** and pay extra van debt only after household bills allow.
After **2036**, take ground-level paid work only if still employed and physically able.
feel: **Anxious** about present money, with more time to prepare.
S4.quote: I cannot use a ten-year warning to pay next month’s garage bill.
fieldNote: The extra debt payment is **new saving from wages**, conditional on Denise’s hours and core bills.
He separates 2026 work from **conditional post-2036 employment**, without claiming a funded early exit.

steps.text: Keep paid cottage loft shifts during 2026
Pay extra van debt from wages only if Denise’s hours and core bills allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could take small cottage jobs by 2031 before Denise and I can afford for me to stop. Posted work with firm travel-and-bills-covering pay and funded paid training would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a course pays a carpenter while he learns. A week without wages could empty what is left for the van.

headlineQuote: A week without wages could empty what is left for the van.
portrait: **Umar**, 58, is a skilled cottage-renovation lead with a trade certificate, low pay and less than one month saved.
Denise’s **part-time garage wage** helps, but van debt, shoulder pain and few local builders limit his choices.
He has never used **AI tools** and would consider robot training only for a posted paid job with funded hours.
The **2028 case** alarms him because 2031 robots might take cottage work before retirement is affordable.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce his low-paid loft work before he can afford retirement.
whatWouldHelp: **Posted work** with firm pay after travel and funded paid training would help.
